The tempting wrong answer — ease the jib sheet — fails because: Dumping the jib first leaves the main's side force intact - the heel and helm come mostly from the main. Tension the boom vang — pin the boom down and hold the leech

e: Slide the jib car forward: Reaching, the lead should follow the clew - moving it forward pulls down on the rising clew so the sail breaks evenly instead of the top luffing first. The tempting wrong answer — sheet the jib in — fails because: Over-sheeting stalls the bottom of the sail completely without fixing the twisted-open top. (Per Quantum Sails, Headsail Trim Guide.)

s: Close-hauled in 16 kt of wind: heeling too far and weather helm developing. Which line do you reach for?

o.t: Tension the boom vang — pin the boom down and hold the leech
Tension the outhaul — stretch the foot flat
Ease the cunningham — let the luff relax and the draft settle
Ease the jib sheet — give the jib room to breathe

e: Tension the outhaul: Add outhaul first - it flattens the lower third of the main and is the first de-powering tool because it disturbs the rest of the sail shape least. The tempting wrong answer — ease the cunningham — fails because: Slacking the luff lets the draft blow further aft, which increases weather helm. (Per Quantum Sails + SailZing, Seven Depowering Tools.)

o.t: Pull the traveler up to windward — bring the boom up without touching twist
Sheet the main in — close the leech and point
Ease the backstay — straighten the mast and power up
Ease the jib sheet — give the jib room to breathe

e: Pull the traveler up to windward: Pulling the traveler car up to weather brings the boom back to the centerline for power and pointing while the soft sheet preserves twist. The tempting wrong answer — sheet the main in — fails because: Sheeting in centers the boom but also pulls down, closing the leech and stalling the sail in light air. (Per Quantum Sails, Mainsail Trim Guide.)

s: On a close reach in 11 kt of wind: a puff hits on the reach; heel and helm surge. Which line do you reach for?

o.t: Ease the mainsheet — open the leech and let the sail breathe
Ease the boom vang — let the boom rise and the top open
Tension the backstay — bend the mast and flatten both sails
Ease the cunningham — let the luff relax and the draft settle

e: Ease the mainsheet: For perfect trim on a reach, ease in every puff - letting the sail luff briefly spills the excess power and keeps the boat on her feet. The tempting wrong answer — ease the boom vang — fails because: On a close reach the sheet is the throttle; dumping the vang gives you an uncontrolled leech and a slower recovery. (Per Quantum Sails, Mainsail Trim Guide.)

s: Close-hauled in 11 kt of wind: boat fully up to speed and starting to heel too much in the puffs; jib entry very round. Which line do you reach for?

o.t: Ease the jib halyard — soften the jib's entry
Ease the outhaul — deepen the lower third of the main
Tension the backstay — bend the mast and flatten both sails
Tension the main halyard — firm up the main's luff

e: Tension the backstay: Once the boat is up to speed and beginning to heel too much, reducing headstay sag flattens the jib and firms the entry to maximize upwind performance. The tempting wrong answer — ease the jib halyard — fails because: A softer luff lets the draft slide aft, making the sail rounder and the heel worse. (Per Quantum Sails, Headsail Trim Guide.)

s: On a close reach in 6 kt of wind: sails strapped in as if beating; boat sluggish on the reach. Which line do you reach for?

o.t: Tension the jib halyard — round the jib's entry
Tension the outhaul — stretch the foot flat
Tension the backstay — bend the mast and flatten both sails
Ease the mainsheet — open the leech and let the sail breathe

e: Ease the mainsheet: On a reach the golden rule is when in doubt, let it out - ease until the luff just bubbles, then trim only enough to stop the luffing. The tempting wrong answer — tension the backstay — fails because: Flattening the sails de-powers a boat that is under-trimmed, not overpowered. (Per Quantum Sails, Mainsail Trim Guide.)

s: Close-hauled in 6 kt of wind: top of the jib twists wide open and the top telltales luff long before the bottom ones. Which line do you reach for?

o.t: Tension the boom vang — pin the boom down and hold the leech
Slide the jib car forward — pull down on the clew and close the jib's top
Ease the backstay — straighten the mast and power up
Tension the jib halyard — round the jib's entry

e: Slide the jib car forward: Moving the lead car forward pulls down on the clew, tensioning the leech and closing the top so the sail luffs evenly; forward lead also powers up the sail in light air. The tempting wrong answer — tension the jib halyard — fails because: Halyard tension moves draft forward but does not close the twisted-open upper leech. (Per Quantum Sails, Headsail Trim Guide.)

s: On a beam reach in 11 kt of wind: sheet eased for the reach and the boom rises; the top of the main dumps open. Which line do you reach for?

o.t: Tension the main halyard — firm up the main's luff
Ease the jib halyard — soften the jib's entry
Sheet the main in — close the leech and point
Tension the boom vang — pin the boom down and hold the leech

e: Tension the boom vang: When the boom goes out, the vang takes over the mainsheet's job of pulling down - use enough vang to keep the top batten parallel to the boom. The tempting wrong answer — sheet the main in — fails because: Re-trimming the sheet closes the top but points the whole sail too close to the wind for the angle, killing speed. (Per Quantum Sails, Mainsail Trim Guide.)

s: On a broad reach in 16 kt of wind: a gust hits on the broad reach; boat overpressed, helm loads up, rail buried. Which line do you reach for?

o.t: Ease the boom vang — let the boom rise and the top open
Slide the jib car forward — pull down on the clew and close the jib's top
Tension the backstay — bend the mast and flatten both sails
Sheet the main in — close the leech and point

e: Ease the boom vang: When overpowered off the wind, easing the vang spills power from the top of the main, reduces heel, and balances the helm. The tempting wrong answer — tension the backstay — fails because: Backstay tension barely changes an eased-out main and does nothing for the immediate gust. (Per North Sails, Downwind Sail Trim.)

s: Close-hauled in 21 kt of wind: overpowered; main full and baggy with the draft past the middle of the sail. Which line do you reach for?

o.t: Ease the outhaul — deepen the lower third of the main
Tension the cunningham — drag the draft forward
Tension the boom vang — pin the boom down and hold the leech
Ease the main halyard — soften the main's luff

e: Tension the cunningham: Progressive cunningham tension as the wind builds hauls the maximum draft back to its proper position, reducing side force and weather helm. The tempting wrong answer — ease the outhaul — fails because: Easing the outhaul adds depth and power to a sail that is already too full. (Per SailZing, Seven Depowering Tools.)

s: Close-hauled in 6 kt of wind: a vertical gutter runs up the main just behind the luff. Which line do you reach for?

o.t: Ease the outhaul — deepen the lower third of the main
Tension the outhaul — stretch the foot flat
Ease the jib halyard — soften the jib's entry
Ease the main halyard — soften the main's luff

e: Ease the main halyard: A vertical wrinkle parallel to the luff is the sign of too much halyard tension; in light air the luff should show just a hint of horizontal wrinkles. The tempting wrong answer — ease the outhaul — fails because: The outhaul works on the foot, not the luff, so the gutter stays. (Per Quantum Sails, Mainsail Trim Guide.)

s: Close-hauled in 6 kt of wind: top telltales stall and disappear behind the leech. Which line do you reach for?

o.t: Tension the cunningham — drag the draft forward
Ease the mainsheet — open the leech and let the sail breathe
Drop the traveler down to leeward — drop the boom to leeward, shape untouched
Ease the backstay — straighten the mast and power up

e: Ease the mainsheet: A deep light-air sail shape is prone to stalling, so it must be trimmed with plenty of twist to keep flow attached up high. The tempting wrong answer — tension the cunningham — fails because: Luff tension moves draft forward but does not open the stalled upper leech. (Per North U (Bill Gladstone), Understanding Twist.)

s: Close-hauled in 11 kt of wind: jib draft drifting aft, wrinkles at the jib luff, steering groove getting narrow. Which line do you reach for?

o.t: Tension the cunningham — drag the draft forward
Slide the jib car aft — flatten the jib's foot and open its top
Tension the jib halyard — round the jib's entry
Slide the jib car forward — pull down on the clew and close the jib's top

e: Tension the jib halyard: Adding halyard tension pulls the draft forward, making the entry rounder and the steering groove wider and more forgiving as the apparent wind increases. The tempting wrong answer — slide the jib car forward — fails because: Moving the car changes leech and foot balance, not luff cloth tension. (Per Quantum Sails, Headsail Trim Guide.)

s: On a close reach in 11 kt of wind: the leeward jib telltale spins and hangs down. Which line do you reach for?

o.t: Ease the outhaul — deepen the lower third of the main
Ease the jib sheet — give the jib room to breathe
Tension the jib halyard — round the jib's entry
Tension the main halyard — firm up the main's luff

e: Ease the jib sheet: A spinning or drooping leeward telltale means the sail is over-trimmed and stalled - ease until the telltales flow straight aft again. The tempting wrong answer — tension the jib halyard — fails because: Luff tension changes draft position but cannot fix an over-sheeted, stalled sail. (Per Quantum Sails, Headsail Trim Guide.)

s: Running downwind in 11 kt of wind: on the run the boom bounces skyward in the waves and the top of the main dumps. Which line do you reach for?

o.t: Sheet the main in — close the leech and point
Tension the jib halyard — round the jib's entry
Tension the boom vang — pin the boom down and hold the leech
Tension the cunningham — drag the draft forward

e: Tension the boom vang: With the boom well outboard the mainsheet can no longer hold the leech, so the vang becomes the twist control - tension it to keep the boom down and the leech stable. The tempting wrong answer — sheet the main in — fails because: Sheeting in cuts projected sail area on a run; the vang, not the sheet, controls the leech out here. (Per UK Sailmakers, Mainsail Trim.)

s: On a beam reach in 11 kt of wind: lower main still flat as a board from the beat; boat feels underpowered on the reach. Which line do you reach for?

o.t: Tension the cunningham — drag the draft forward
Ease the outhaul — deepen the lower third of the main
Slide the jib car forward — pull down on the clew and close the jib's top
Ease the boom vang — let the boom rise and the top open

e: Ease the outhaul: The outhaul is eased off when sailing off the wind, adding depth and power to the lower third - upwind flat, off the wind full. The tempting wrong answer — tension the cunningham — fails because: More luff tension flattens and de-powers a sail that needs depth for the reach. (Per Quantum Sails, Mainsail Trim Guide.)

s: Close-hauled in 16 kt of wind: every time the sheet is eased in a gust the boom skies and the top of the main dumps. Which line do you reach for?

o.t: Ease the main halyard — soften the main's luff
Slide the jib car aft — flatten the jib's foot and open its top
Pull the traveler up to windward — bring the boom up without touching twist
Tension the boom vang — pin the boom down and hold the leech

e: Tension the boom vang: In heavy air upwind the vang helps the mainsheet hold the boom down, keeping leech tension so the sheet can be eased without the whole top twisting off - vang sheeting. The tempting wrong answer — pull the traveler up to windward — fails because: Pulling the boom back up to weather adds side force and heel just when you are trying to shed it. (Per Quantum Sails, Mainsail Trim Guide.)

s: Close-hauled in 6 kt of wind: jib luff is bar-tight with a rounded entry and the boat feels dead. Which line do you reach for?

o.t: Ease the boom vang — let the boom rise and the top open
Ease the jib halyard — soften the jib's entry
Sheet the jib in — trim the jib closer
Tension the boom vang — pin the boom down and hold the leech

e: Ease the jib halyard: In light apparent wind the jib halyard should be soft enough to leave just a hint of horizontal wrinkles - over-tension pulls the draft too far forward and hurts light-air performance. The tempting wrong answer — sheet the jib in — fails because: Sheeting harder does nothing for the over-tight luff and risks stalling the sail in light air. (Per Quantum Sails, Headsail Trim Guide.)

s: On a beam reach in 6 kt of wind: vang still strapped on from the beat; leech hooked and lifeless on the light-air reach. Which line do you reach for?

o.t: Sheet the jib in — trim the jib closer
Sheet the main in — close the leech and point
Ease the boom vang — let the boom rise and the top open
Slide the jib car aft — flatten the jib's foot and open its top

e: Ease the boom vang: Light air demands twist - easing the vang lets the upper leech open so flow stays attached to the deep, easily-stalled light-air shape. The tempting wrong answer — sheet the jib in — fails because: Strapping the jib does nothing for the hooked main leech and stalls the slot. (Per North U (Bill Gladstone), Understanding Twist.)

s: Close-hauled in 6 kt of wind: lower main looks flat and lifeless; boat has no punch. Which line do you reach for?

Ease the main halyard — soften the main's luff
Tension the cunningham — drag the draft forward
Ease the outhaul — deepen the lower third of the main

e: Ease the outhaul: Easing the outhaul adds depth and power to the lower third of the main, which is what you want in light-to-moderate conditions when you need power and helm feel. The tempting wrong answer — tension the cunningham — fails because: Hauling the luff flattens and de-powers the sail further instead of adding the depth you need. (Per Quantum Sails, Mainsail Trim Guide.)

s: Close-hauled in 6 kt of wind: leech looks clamped shut and hooked; boat will not accelerate in the light patches. Which line do you reach for?

o.t: Tension the cunningham — drag the draft forward
Ease the boom vang — let the boom rise and the top open
Tension the outhaul — stretch the foot flat
Ease the jib sheet — give the jib room to breathe

e: Ease the boom vang: In light air you minimize downward boom tension - vang off, light sheet - so the leech can open naturally and the sail carries the extra twist light air demands. The tempting wrong answer — tension the outhaul — fails because: Flattening the foot removes power without addressing the closed, stalled leech. (Per SailZing, Controlling Twist.)

s: On a broad reach in 6 kt of wind: main hauled too close for the angle; boat glides to a stop. Which line do you reach for?

o.t: Tension the boom vang — pin the boom down and hold the leech
Ease the mainsheet — open the leech and let the sail breathe
Tension the backstay — bend the mast and flatten both sails
Sheet the jib in — trim the jib closer

e: Ease the mainsheet: When in doubt, let it out - ease until the sail begins to luff, even until it rests against the shrouds and spreaders, provided the vang is on enough. The tempting wrong answer — tension the boom vang — fails because: In light air hard vang clamps the leech shut and kills what little flow the sail has. (Per Quantum Sails, Mainsail Trim Guide.)

s: Close-hauled in 21 kt of wind: constant heavy weather helm and rounding up in gusts even after flattening everything. Which line do you reach for?

o.t: Pull the traveler up to windward — bring the boom up without touching twist
Tuck in a reef — shorten sail and drop the center of effort

e: Tuck in a reef: When the de-powering tweaks are exhausted, shortening the mainsail lowers the center of effort and restores helm balance - and a reefed boat sails more upright and often just as fast. The tempting wrong answer — tension the cunningham — fails because: The cunningham is already maxed by this point and cannot compensate for carrying too much sail area. (Per SAIL Magazine, The Line on Reefing.)

e: Tension the backstay: Backstay tension bends the mast, pulling the luff away from the leech and flattening the upper two-thirds of the main - a flatter sail heels less and carries less weather helm. The tempting wrong answer — ease the main halyard — fails because: Softening the luff moves the draft aft and deepens the sail, the opposite of what an overpowered boat needs.
